newsitem.title: FRANCE: Protesters mass against French far-right congress.
newsitem.headline: Protesters mass against French far-right congress.

text.p: Members of France's far-right National Front, hoping for an election breakthrough next year, gathered for their congress on Saturday amid heavy security as thousands of foes massed nearby for a protest march.

Row upon row of riot police, and the party's own burly security guards, sealed off the conference centre in the reluctant host city of Strasbourg as Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen arrived for the three-day meeting.
"We believe that if the French people knew what we truly think -- and not the caricature provided by our adversaries -- we would have a majority, as in Vitrolles," Le Pen, 68, said.
The Front was buoyed by winning the Vitrolles city hall in a municipal by-election last month, the fourth town it controls in southern France after Toulon, Orange and Marignane.

Strasbourg's Socialist mayor Catherine Trautmann has called in 2,000 police and appealed for calm even as she vowed to lead the protest, which organisers said would draw more than 50,000 people from across the country, Germany and Switzerland.
The march was due to start at 3 p.m. (1400 GMT), half an hour after the congress opening..

As protesters poured in on chartered "freedom trains" and buses, Front leaders advised the 2,200 delegates to remain closeted in the congress and warned authorities they would responsible for any violence.
"They are trying to frighten us, but we won't respond," said 20-year old Front delegate Laetitia Firek.
A red flag with a swastika was briefly hoisted on the spire of the towering Gothic cathedral as local officials visited the site of a synagogue burnt down by the Nazis in World War Two.
Representatives of the MRAP anti-racist group lay a wreath at the site of the Struthof Nazi World War Two concentration camp, near Strasbourg, where some 25,000 died.

Giant city hall posters in various languages outside the congress centre proclaimed the motto of the French Republic "liberty, equality, fraternity". Anti-Front protesters, saying they were "mourning democracy", planted black flowers, painted black bands on street signs and blindfolded statues in black.
The Strasbourg march caps a groundswell of opposition to Le Pen which was fuelled by the Front victory in Vitrolles.
The feisty Le Pen, who won 15 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential poll, has vowed an assault on the political establishment in the run-up to a March 1998 general election.
The Front calls for sending immigrants home and giving preference to French nationals for jobs and social benefits.

France's first-past-the-post election system has barred the Front from parliament, but delegates sounded confident it can ride to power on record 12.8 percent unemployment and simmering resentment of North African immigrants and political corruption.
A survey in the weekly Le Point said that the Front would poll 15 percent of the votes, up from 12.5 percent in 1993, but would remain out of parliament if the election was held now.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin and Communist chief Robert Hue, who were to take part in the protest march, denounced the Front in interviews published by the daily Le Parisien on Saturday, as racist, xenophobic, anti-Semitic and fascist.

Politicians disagree on how to counter the Front's rise, with the ruling centre-right coalition refusing to participate in the march and President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist Rally for the Republic arguing that protests played into Le Pen's hands.
Many analysts agreed that the protests would mainly serve to keep the Front and its controversial agenda in the public eye.

The congress is to re-elect Le Pen as president, choose a central committee and draft an election platform and campaign strategy. The party's founder, Le Pen is unopposed and has refused to discuss a successor.
The previous National Front congress, held in suburban Paris five years ago, adopted a platform of "300 measures for the rebirth of France".
